I went on a school trip once, and I got lost.

I ran.

A shadow stood motionless behind me. Not chasing. Just there.

After hours of wandering through alien, twisting woods, my foot hit a familiar root. I knew this spot. I stopped. My heart, which had been pounding with fear, now hammered with something else—hope, maybe.

I didn't trust it. I listened, waiting for the forest to trick me. But there was only silence.

Then a voice called my name.

I opened my mouth. Nothing came out at first—my throat was raw from holding back fear. But I shouted, voice cracking: "Here! I'm here!"

Branches rustled. A figure emerged from the darkness. It was my teacher. He looked pale, exhausted. He had been searching all night.

For a long moment, neither of us spoke.

Then he said, "You're alive."

She knew which trees along Main Street bloomed first in spring, and the exact sound the town bell made at noon — deep and unhurried, like the place itself. Her hometown wasn't just a dot on a map. She loved this town. She loved the way Mrs. Herrera waved from her porch every evening, the way the library smelled of old paper and dust, the way every face on every street was familiar. This place had raised her. It had held her when she fell, celebrated her small victories, and wrapped her in a warmth that felt eternal.

The Lad Who Had a Lap (An Essay)

There was once a lad who had a lap. Not a lap of luxury, not a lap around the track — a lap that was his, a place where something rested. The lad was proud of his lap. He kept it warm, kept it ready. And on that lap sat something that loved to larp.

Every weekend, the lap would dress up. Armor made of cardboard. Spells made of shout. It would go into the woods with others who also believed — really believed — that they were elves, knights, wizards. The lap came home tired, covered in fake mud and real joy. And the lad would hold that lap and say nothing. Because what was there to say? The lap believed.

Now here is the strange thing: the lad was not a lad. That much became clear over time. The lad had a voice too soft, a stance too still, a way of watching that did not belong to a lad. But the lap never noticed. Or if it did, it never said. The lap was too busy larping.

And so the lad who was not a lad carried the lap who loved to larp through life. Through grocery stores, through quiet evenings, through the long years where the world got louder and louder. The world began to shout: Be what you say you are. Perform. Declare. Let everyone see your truth.

But the lad — the non-lad — grew quieter.

Because the lad had learned something that the lap had not: the mask you wear is still a mask, even if you forget you're wearing it.

The lap larped as a hero. But the lad knew — you cannot save yourself. The lap larped as a mage. But the lad knew — there is only one power that does not fade. The lap larped as a fighter. But the lad knew — the real battle is not in the woods on a Saturday.

It is in the quiet, in the stillness, in the moment when all the costumes fall away and you are just a soul. Naked. Known. Seen.

One day the lap came home and said, "I think I want to larp forever. I think I want to be the elf. I think I am the elf."

And the lad — who was not a lad — finally spoke.

"You are not the elf. You are not the knight. You are not the mage. You are a creature made by a Creator. And you are loved. Not for the role you play. Not for the name you choose. But because you are His."

The lap looked at the lad. For the first time, really looked.

"Who are you?" the lap asked.

And the lad smiled. And said nothing.

Because some messages are not meant to be spoken. They are meant to be uncovered — like a seed buried under snow, waiting for spring, waiting for the right heart to find it, waiting for the lap to finally stop larping long enough to look up.

Breaking the curse was not simple.

She didn't know how.

"You were the only thing I ever did right," she whispered. "The only thing that made me feel like I mattered."

"Then let me go," Lena said. "And you can find out if you matter on your own."

The word was spoken in a whisper, so soft Lena almost didn't hear it.

But she did.

Part Five: The After

She spoke the word at midnight, under an open sky.

The curse broke like a bone snapping.

She felt everything drain out of her — the mathematics, the music, the languages, the impossible lightning speed of her own mind. She felt herself become smaller, softer, ordinary.

It was terrifying.

And it was freeing.

She collapsed, and Aliasse caught her.

"I don't know," she said. "But I'm me."

Aliasse held her tighter.

"Yeah," she said. "You are."

One year later.

She was average.

And she had never been happier.

"You were the one who broke the curse."

And she thought about this: sitting in a coffee shop with a friend, no curse between them, just two ordinary people.

"No," she said. "I don't."

And she meant it.
